newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: U.S. military official visits OAU headquarters.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military official visits OAU headquarters.

text.p: A senior U.S. military commander visited on Wednesday the Conflict Management Centre, set up to check conflicts on the world's poorest continent, at the headquarters of the Organisation of African Unity.

General James Jamerson, deputy commander-in-chief of the U.S. European Command, also held talks with Ahmed Haggag, the acting secretary-general of the OAU, during which they reviewed conflict situations on the continent.
OAU officials said the U.S.-funded centre is fully computerised and includes an early warning system that would be used to monitor conflicts in Africa on a 24-hour basis.
The visit to the OAU by Jamerson comes ahead of one from U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher next week.
OAU officials said it was possible Jamerson may also have discussed with Haggag an American proposal to train and equip an African intervention force.

The Washington Post said on Saturday President Bill Clinton had approved an ambitious plan to organise, train, equip and help deploy an all-African force of 10,000 troops to intervene in African crises.
Christopher was expected to discuss the African Crisis Response Force (ACRF) plan with African leaders during his trip.
Assistant Secretary of State for Africa George Moose toured Africa last week to solicit troop commitments from Zimbabwe, Botswana, Ethiopia, Uganda, Tanzania, Kenya and Mozambique.
The Washington Post said the ACRF would be sent to countries where insurrection, civil war or campaigns of genocide threatened mass civilian casualties.
The ACRF would not intervene in the fighting but would establish and protect safe areas where civilians could gather and receive humanitarian assistance, according to the report.
U.S. officials estimate it would cost $25 million to set up the force and a further $40 million if the force was deployed.
The United States was prepared to pick up half the cost and was counting on European allies to come up with the rest in cash, equipment or training, officials told the Washington Post.
The OAU has not mounted a peace force since it sent a force to Chad in the 1980s which was forced to withdraw in confusion because of uncertainty about its role.
The organisation has been powerless to stop Africa's endless civil wars including genocide in the tiny central African state of Rwanda, where a million people were slaughtered in 1994.
